metadata.title: Teachers Collaborating as a Professional Learning Network and Learning How to Implement Collaborative Problem Solving in the Primary Math’s Classroom

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a qualitative case study of a small teacher team in one local public/state primary school in NSW, Australia, using focus-group and interview data plus teacher reflections. It does not use ILSA microdata (e.g., PISA student achievement PVs) and therefore does not require plausible-value handling or complex survey weighting for student achievement estimation. Because the analysis is thematic and based on recorded/transcribed teacher discussions, there is no sampling frame for students and no design-weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) to apply. Consequently, survey weights and replicate weights are not part of the analytic workflow.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not analyze cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA assessment (e.g., PISA/CPS achievement PVs). Instead, the dependent material is teachers’ perceptions and reflections captured through focus-group transcripts and reflective observation proformas. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not describe a quantitative student-level dataset with missing entries requiring imputation or deletion rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Case study design: five primary teachers (classes of students aged 10–12) from one local public/state primary school in NSW, Australia. Teachers participated in two after-school professional learning sessions on CPS and then implemented at least one CPS maths lesson per week, providing weekly oral reflections to the researcher. The paper’s reported results focus on the final focus-group session data (recorded and transcribed) from the whole teacher team; individual interview and reflection data are discussed as explored in other papers.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict problem solving, finding that This paper reports a qualitative case study rather than an empirical ML prediction study. It examines how a small team of five primary teachers in one NSW public/state school used a professional learning network (PLN) and an action-research cycle to implement collaborative problem solving (CPS) in primary mathematics. Data come from a focus-group session (recorded and transcribed) and teacher reflections, analyzed using reflective thematic analysis, yielding five themes: Collaborative Leadership, Common Vision, Collective Vision with Students, Trust, and Deeper Understanding of CL and CPS. No quantitative performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, RMSE, AUC) are reported because there is no model training or predictive target. The study is not generalisable beyond the single school context, and it does not use ILSA microdata or survey-weighted estimation. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript is not an empirical large-scale assessment analysis and does not train or evaluate any machine learning models. It is a qualitative case study using thematic analysis of teacher perceptions, so fields required for ML prediction (dataset-based targets, PV handling, missing-data strategy for student records, and numeric model performance) are not applicable or not reported.
